name: Dana Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage a beef farm for an older couple, the Fairbairns, who are winding down. We've got 150 suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves on grass, and about 80 hectares we cut for hay. Mornings I check the cattle, afternoons depend on the season, and in summer it's all hay: mowing, turning, baling, and praying it doesn't rain for four days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the side of it you enjoy?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hay business, honestly. I started selling small bales to horse owners three years ago, and now it's a third of the farm's income. I run the whole thing off my phone. An AI app helps me price it, write the adverts, and keep track of who's paid. Mr Fairbairn calls it my 'hay empire'.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thin money. My pay's low, and I put everything spare back into the hay side, a second-hand bale wrapper last spring. Ben, my partner, is an electrician, and his work's steady, thank God. We've got a couple of weeks of bills in the bank. Not a lot of room if something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool and anyone running a small business should use it. I'd probably post about how I run the hay orders with it, because other farmers always ask. I'd say it's the best free business help I've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's what I've already got, so no big change. Cattle prices and the weather still matter more. But it does make me feel I can run a proper business without paying an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the AI further: use it to track the cattle's weight gain and plan when to sell. I'd add a delivery booking system for the hay. Maybe try selling some beef direct to the horse customers, since they already trust me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. This one suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling beef to horse owners. Do horse people want beef?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You'd be surprised. Half of them already ask about it when they pick up hay. One lady, Mrs Osei, has been on at me for a year about a quarter of beef for her freezer. I've just never had time to set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your faith or your family say about all this business talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say don't forget Sunday. I don't. Church in the morning, cattle check in the afternoon. The hay can wait one day a week, and the customers know it.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a great tool and anyone running a small business should use it. I'd post about how I run my hay orders with it, because other farmers always ask.
S0.think: It's what I've already got, so no big change, and cattle prices and the weather still matter more. But it lets me run a proper business without paying for an office.
S0.do: Uses AI to track cattle weight gain and plan sales, and adds a delivery booking system for hay. Tries selling beef direct to her hay customers, starting with one who has asked for a year.
S0.feel: Calm and a little excited; this suits her.
S0.quote: The hay can wait one day a week, and the customers know it.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is a natural small-business builder who uses AI daily, held steady by church and family. She sees AI as freeing her from needing an office, which fits her free-market outlook. She already has customers waiting for products she hasn't had time to launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's up to people to keep up, and up to businesses to train them properly. Apprenticeships, not schemes. I'd say farms should be allowed to take on young people without a mountain of forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow change suits me. I'm ahead, and I'll stay ahead. The only worry is if I need help, fewer young people will have been trained. Mr Fairbairn's grandson might want to come back, but he's in an office in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a school leaver for the summer hay, paid properly, and teach them the cattle too. I'd try the newest AI tools as they come out and drop the ones that don't pay. I'd set up the beef box sales properly by the autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'apprenticeships, not schemes'. What's the difference to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprenticeship is a real job with a real boss who teaches you. A scheme is a government form and a certificate. I've seen lads come out of schemes who can't reverse a trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the grandson comes back and wants to run things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to find my place. It's their farm, not mine. I'd hope he'd see the hay business and want me running it. If not, I'd take my customers and find some land to rent. That's the risk of building on someone else's ground.

S1.say: I'd say it's up to people to keep up and up to businesses to train them properly, through apprenticeships, not schemes. Farms should be able to take on young people without a mountain of forms.
S1.think: Slow change suits me because I'm ahead and I'll stay ahead. My only worry is that fewer young people will be trained if I need help.
S1.do: Takes on a school leaver for the summer hay at proper pay and teaches them cattle work. Tries new AI tools and drops those that don't pay, and launches beef box sales by autumn.
S1.quote: I've seen lads come out of schemes who can't reverse a trailer.
S1.fieldNote: She is confident about change itself but quietly aware that she is building on land she doesn't own. The owners' grandson returning is her real long-term risk. Her view of training is firmly practical and employer-led.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get back on their feet, and the new jobs are there for people willing to learn. I'd say the politicians should stop arguing and make it easy to start a small business. That's what I'd want if I were laid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it might hurt the hay side. Horse owners are often office people with money to spare. If they lose jobs, the horses go first, or at least the expensive hay does. I'd watch the orders closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the AI to sort my customers by job and how likely they are to cut back, which sounds cold, but it's business. I'd offer cheaper bulk deals and a monthly payment plan. And I'd quietly look for horse livery yards, the places that keep horses for owners, to sell to in bulk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But it's the kind of uneasy I can do something about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sorting customers by how likely they are to cut back. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, honestly. Mrs Osei is a lovely woman, and I'd hate to think of her as a number. But if I don't plan for the dip, I'm the one who goes under, and then nobody gets hay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ben's work be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I think. People still need electricians. If anything, he'd get busier, wiring up all the new computer stuff in offices. That's what keeps me calm, knowing one of us is steady.

S2.say: I'd say people should get back on their feet and the new jobs are there for those willing to learn. Politicians should stop arguing and make it easy to start a small business.
S2.think: It might hurt the hay business, because many horse owners are office workers with money to spare. If they lose jobs, the expensive hay goes first.
S2.do: Uses AI to sort hay customers by how likely they are to cut back and offers bulk deals and monthly payment plans. Looks for horse livery yards to sell to in bulk.
S2.feel: Uneasy, but the kind she feels she can act on.
S2.quote: Mrs Osei is a lovely woman, and I'd hate to think of her as a number.
S2.fieldNote: Her business brain goes straight to sorting customers, and she admits it feels cold. Her partner's steady trade work is what keeps her calm. She'd want help starting businesses rather than benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who've made money should invest it back into the country and their communities, and the government shouldn't grab it all and waste it. I'd say physical work has always been the backbone. I'd post that, probably, and get some arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this could be good for me. House and share prices booming means rich people buying land and horses. More horses, more hay. And they'll pay for good local beef. But the Fairbairns might be tempted to sell the farm while land is high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd raise hay prices for the new customers and keep them steady for the old ones. I'd talk to the Fairbairns about renting me part of the land long-term before anyone else offers. I'd take a small loan for a second baler if the orders were there. And I'd ask the AI to help me write a proper business plan for the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and anxious at the same time. Doing well while people are losing jobs feels a bit wrong, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan, with a couple of weeks of savings. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. I'd only do it if the orders were already in, written down, paid for in part. Ben would want to see the numbers. He's the careful one, and I'm glad of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said doing well while others lose jobs feels a bit wrong. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give some hay free to the riding school for disabled kids in town. They're always scraping by. And I'd hire someone local who'd lost their office job, if they wanted outside work.

S3.say: I'd say people who've made money should invest it back into the country and their communities, and the government shouldn't grab it and waste it. Physical work has always been the backbone.
S3.think: This could be good for me, as newly rich people buy land and horses and pay for local beef. But the owners might sell the farm while land prices are high.
S3.do: Raises hay prices for new customers only, and asks the owners for a long-term lease on part of the land. Takes a small loan for a second baler only once orders are in writing, with an AI-drafted business plan.
S3.feel: Excited and anxious, and a little uneasy about doing well while others lose jobs.
S3.quote: I'd give some hay free to the riding school for disabled kids in town. They're always scraping by.
S3.fieldNote: She sees the boom as a business chance, which sets her apart from most farmers in this study. Her thin savings make her careful about debt, and her partner acts as a brake. Her response to feeling uneasy is local charity, not policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots are coming and farmers should get ahead of them, not complain. I'd say the government should keep out and let businesses sort it. And I'd say we still need people who know animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd want one. A robot that could feed cattle and stack bales would free me to grow the hay side. But Ben's an electrician, and building sites are on the list. If robots wire houses, his steady work isn't steady anymore, and that frightens me more than anything on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lease a robot as soon as there was a good one, through the dealer, so I'm not buying it outright. I'd use it on the hay first. I'd push Ben to move into fixing and installing the robots themselves, since someone's got to wire them up. And I'd keep the beef boxes going because people still want to buy from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, mostly for Ben. For me, it's half scary, half the best thing that could happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should keep out. What if Ben lost his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say help him retrain, through the trade, through the firms. Not a benefit cheque. But I'd be lying if I said I'd turn down help if we were desperate. Pride's easy when the money's coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing that would go if Ben's work stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan on the bale wrapper would be the first thing I'd worry about. Then the house. We rent, so it's not the end of the world, but we'd be on my wage, and it's not built for two.

S4.say: I'd say robots are coming and farmers should get ahead of them, not complain. The government should keep out and let businesses sort it, though we'll still need people who know animals.
S4.think: I'd want a robot to free me for the hay business. But if robots can wire houses, Ben's steady electrician work isn't steady anymore, and that frightens me more than anything on the farm.
S4.do: Leases a robot through the dealer as soon as a good one exists and uses it on hay first. Pushes her partner to move into installing and repairing robots, and keeps beef box sales going.
S4.feel: Alarmed for her partner, and half scared, half excited for herself.
S4.quote: Pride's easy when the money's coming in.
S4.fieldNote: The robot scenario flips her household's safety, because her partner's trade work was the steady half. She admits her views on government help might bend if they were desperate. For herself, she still sees robots as a chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because of Ben. He's our steady one. What would help is training for trades people to move into the robot work, run by the trades, not by government offices. And leasing deals so small farmers can get the machines too, not just the big estates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about land. I'm building a business on someone else's farm. If the Fairbairns sell, all of it goes. That's my real worry most nights, not the robots.

headlineQuote: Pride's easy when the money's coming in.
portrait: Dana Mensah is 27 and manages a 150-cow beef farm for an older couple, the Fairbairns, while building her own hay business for horse owners, living with her partner Ben, an electrician. She's energetic, churchgoing and business-minded, uses AI every day to run orders and prices, and prefers apprenticeships and enterprise to government help. She sees opportunity in most scenarios, even the boom, though she admits it feels wrong to do well while others struggle. The robot scenario frightens her mainly because it threatens Ben's steady trade work, and she concedes that pride about help is easy when money is coming in. Her deepest worry is that she's building on land she doesn't own.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because robots on building sites would threaten Ben's electrician work, the steady half of their income.
whatWouldHelp: Training run by the trades to move workers into robot work, and leasing deals so small farmers can get machines too.
